moments.title: Edict of Milan
moments.body: After Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (October 312), he and Licinius issue the Edict of Milan granting religious toleration across the Roman Empire. Christianity, persecuted intermittently for nearly three centuries, becomes legal.
moments.takeaway: Constantine's policy was not yet full imperial sponsorship of Christianity, but the legal change made bishops powerful figures.

moments.title: Council of Nicaea
moments.body: Constantine convenes the first ecumenical council at Nicaea (now İznik, Turkey) to settle the Arian controversy — whether the Son was co-eternal with the Father, or a created being. The Council condemns Arius and produces the Nicene Creed affirming the Son as 'of one substance' (homoousios) with the Father.

quote.text: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of all things visible and invisible.

moments.takeaway: Nicaea did NOT decide the canon of Scripture — a persistent modern myth. It settled the Christological question that defines mainstream Christianity to this day.

moments.title: Council of Constantinople
moments.body: The First Council of Constantinople expanded the Nicene Creed (the version most commonly recited today is technically the 'Niceno-Constantinopolitan' Creed). The Edict of Thessalonica (380) had made Nicene Christianity the state religion of the Roman Empire.
moments.takeaway: By the late 4th century, Nicene Trinitarian Christianity was orthodox state religion. Arianism survived among Germanic peoples (Goths, Vandals) for centuries.

now.title: Nicaea's enduring shape
now.body:
The Nicene Creed remains the most widely shared Christian statement of faith — recited by Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans and many Protestants. The Filioque clause ('and the Son') was added by Western churches in the 6th-11th centuries and became one of the issues splitting Western and Eastern Christianity in 1054.

Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code' (2003) repeated the false claim that Nicaea decided the biblical canon. The 27-book New Testament was settled gradually through the 4th-5th centuries, first listed in its current form by Athanasius's Easter Letter of 367.
now.open_questions: How much of Nicaea was politics, and how much theology? Constantine wanted unity; bishops also wanted theological clarity. Most modern scholars see both motives as real and intertwined.

reflection: Christian orthodoxy is shaped by specific councils with specific political pressures. The Trinitarian theology that defines mainstream Christianity was hammered out in the 4th century — not from the New Testament directly but from centuries of theological argument under imperial pressure.
